title: Initialize a repository
description: Every Git project starts with a single command that turns a plain folder into a repository. Git creates a hidden `.git` folder that stores your entire project history. Run this command inside your workspace folder `/data/repo`.
hint: The command is two words: `git` and a verb meaning 'start from scratch'.

title: Make your first commit
description: A commit is a permanent snapshot of your project. Three steps are always required: create a file (any name, any content), stage it so Git knows to include it, then record the snapshot with a message. Do all your work inside `/data/repo`.
hint: Three commands: create a file (`echo 'hello' > file.txt`), stage it (`git add file.txt`), save it (`git commit -m 'your message'`).

title: Make a second commit
description: A repository becomes useful when it has a history. Modify a file or create a new one, then stage it and commit again. Having at least two commits means you can compare changes, revert, or explore history.
hint: Modify `file.txt` or create a new file, then `git add` and `git commit -m 'second commit'`.

title: Understand repository status
description: Git constantly tracks the difference between your last commit and your working directory. Modify a file you have already committed, then ask Git what it sees. This command tells you what is staged, what is modified, and what Git is not tracking.
hint: Modify a tracked file, then run `git status` — the two-word command that shows what has changed.

title: Ignore files with .gitignore
description: Sometimes you have files you never want Git to track — like compiled binaries, logs, or secrets. Create a file named `.gitignore` and add `secret.txt` to it on its own line. Then create a file named `secret.txt`. Git will pretend it does not exist.
hint: Run `echo secret.txt > .gitignore`. Create the file with `touch secret.txt`. Check `git status` — you won't see `secret.txt` listed.

title: View the commit history
description: Every project has a log — a timeline of every snapshot ever committed. The log shows the commit hash, author, date, and message for each commit. This is how you trace what changed, when, and why. Run the command to view your commit history.
hint: Run `git log` to see full history. Run `git log --oneline` for a compact one-line-per-commit view.

title: Inspect staged changes before committing
description: Before committing, it is good practice to review exactly what you are about to save. Modify a tracked file, stage it with `git add`, and then view the exact line-by-line differences of what is staged compared to the last commit.
hint: Run `git add <file>` to stage changes. Then run `git diff --cached` to see what is staged.

title: Inspect a specific commit
description: You can inspect exactly what changed in any commit — what files were touched, what lines were added or removed. This is essential for code review and debugging. Examine the most recent commit in detail.
hint: Run `git show HEAD` to see all changes in the latest commit. Use `git show <hash>` for any specific commit.

title: Create a branch named 'dev'
description: Branches let you work on something new without touching the stable version. Think of a branch as a parallel timeline — experiment freely, merge back if it works, discard if it does not. Create a branch called exactly `dev`.
hint: Two ways: `git branch dev` creates it without switching. `git checkout -b dev` creates and switches. Either works here.

title: Switch to the 'dev' branch
description: Creating a branch does not move you there. You need to explicitly switch so that your next commits land on `dev` and not on `main`. After switching, new commits are isolated to `dev` — `main` stays untouched until you decide to merge.
hint: Use `git checkout dev` or `git switch dev`. Confirm with `git branch` — the current branch has a star next to it.

title: Merge 'dev' into 'main'
description: Merging brings work from one branch into another. The key rule: you merge INTO the branch you are currently on. To bring `dev` into `main`, switch to `main` first, then run the merge. Make sure `dev` has at least one commit that `main` does not.
hint: Switch to `main` first. Add a commit on `dev` if you have not already. Then `git merge dev` from `main`.

title: Amend the last commit
description: Forgot to include a file or made a typo in your last commit message? Instead of creating a new commit, you can amend the previous one. Modify a file, stage it, and use `--amend` to fold it into the previous commit without creating a new one.
hint: Stage a file with `git add`, then run `git commit --amend --no-edit` to fold changes into the last commit. Or use `git commit --amend -m 'new message'` to also change the message.

title: Stash your changes
description: Stashing saves your uncommitted work to a temporary stack and gives you a clean working directory. This is useful when you need to switch context without making a half-finished commit. Modify a tracked file (do not commit it), then stash it.
hint: Edit a tracked file. Then `git stash`. Check `git stash list` to confirm it saved.

title: Retrieve stashed changes
description: Now that you have safely stashed your changes, retrieve them. `git stash pop` applies the stashed changes back to your working directory AND removes them from the stash stack. Your work is back as if nothing happened.
hint: Run `git stash pop`. Check `git stash list` — it should now be empty. Check `git status` — your changes are back.

title: Rename a branch
description: Sometimes a branch name no longer makes sense as a feature evolves. You can rename it without losing any commits. Create a new branch named `old-name`, then rename it to `feature-login`.
hint: Create a branch with `git branch old-name`. Then rename it with `git branch -m old-name feature-login`. Confirm with `git branch`.

title: Tag a release point
description: Tags mark specific commits as significant milestones — usually software releases. Unlike branches, tags never move as you add more commits. Create a tag named exactly `v1.0` on your current commit.
hint: Use `git tag v1.0`. The name must be exactly `v1.0` — the validator checks for this exact string.

title: Create multiple tags
description: Real projects have many release tags — one per version. You already have `v1.0`. Now create a second tag named `v1.1` to simulate tagging a new release. You should have at least 2 tags total.
hint: Run `git tag v1.1`. Check all your tags with `git tag --list`.

title: Delete the 'dev' branch
description: Once a branch is merged, keeping it around is clutter. Deleting a branch removes the label, not the commits — those are already safely in `main`. Delete the `dev` branch.
hint: Switch to `main` first. Then `git branch -d dev`. Since `dev` is already merged, `-d` (safe delete) works. Use `-D` only if it refuses.

title: Blame a file
description: `git blame` shows you who last modified each line of a file and in which commit. It is essential for tracking down when a bug was introduced and by whom. Run `git blame` on a file that has been committed.
hint: Make sure you have a committed file (e.g., `file.txt`). Then run `git blame file.txt`. Each line shows the commit hash, author, date, and the line content.

title: Summarize commit history with shortlog
description: `git shortlog` groups commits by author and shows a count of contributions. This is a quick way to see who has contributed most to a project. Run it to get a contribution summary.
hint: Run `git shortlog -s HEAD` to see a summary of commit counts per author. Or just `git shortlog HEAD` for the full list.

title: Rebase a branch onto main
description: Rebase replays your branch's commits on top of another branch's latest commit, producing a clean straight line — no merge commits. Create a branch called `feature`, add at least one commit on it, then rebase it onto `main`.
hint: While on `feature`, run `git rebase main`. Check the result with `git log --oneline --graph`.

title: Revert a commit safely
description: When you make a mistake on a shared branch, you should NOT rewrite history because others may have already pulled it. Instead, use `git revert` — this creates a brand new commit that undoes a previous one, keeping history intact.
hint: Run `git revert HEAD`. A text editor might pop up to confirm the commit message — just save and close it (`Ctrl+X` in nano, `:wq` in vim).

title: Cherry-pick a single commit
description: Cherry-pick copies one specific commit from one branch and applies it onto another as a new commit with a different hash. Useful when you want just one fix from a feature branch without merging everything. Find a commit hash on `feature`, switch to `main`, and apply only that commit.
hint: Use `git log feature --oneline` to find the hash. Then on `main`: `git cherry-pick <hash>`. The new commit will have a different SHA than the original.

title: Hard reset to a previous commit
description: If you want to completely discard recent commits AND uncommitted changes, returning your branch exactly to a previous state, use a hard reset. WARNING: this permanently deletes uncommitted work. Reset your branch back by one commit.
hint: Run `git reset --hard HEAD~1` to move the current branch back by exactly one commit, discarding all changes. Use `git log --oneline` before and after to see the difference.

title: Interactive rebase to clean history
description: Interactive rebase (`git rebase -i`) lets you rewrite history before sharing it — squash multiple commits into one, reorder them, or edit messages. Make at least 2 commits on your current branch, then use interactive rebase to combine (squash) them or reword a message.
hint: Run `git rebase -i HEAD~2` to enter interactive mode for the last 2 commits. In the editor, change `pick` to `squash` (or `s`) on the second line to squash it into the first.

title: Write a conventional commit message
description: Good commit messages follow a convention that makes the log readable for everyone. The Conventional Commits format is `<type>: <short summary>` — e.g., `feat: add login button`, `fix: correct off-by-one error`, `docs: update README`. Make a commit whose message starts with `feat:`.
hint: Run `git commit -m 'feat: add new feature'`. The message must start with `feat:` (lowercase). Check with `git log -1 --format=%s`.

title: Clone from the practice remote
description: This platform runs its own internal git-server — no internet required. A bare repository has been set up for you. Clone it using this URL (replace `<your-reg-no>` with your registration number): `git://git-server/<your-reg-no>/practice.git`. Run from inside `/data/repo`. You will get a `practice` subfolder — do the next tasks inside that folder.
hint: From `/data/repo`, run: `git clone git://git-server/<your-reg-no>/practice.git`. The 'empty repository' warning is normal — the remote starts empty.

title: Push commits to the remote
description: Pushing sends your local commits to the remote repository. Work inside the cloned `practice` folder: create a file, commit it, then push to origin. After pushing, your local `main` and `origin/main` should point to the same commit.
hint: Navigate into the `practice` folder first. Then: create a file, `git add`, `git commit -m 'message'`, `git push origin main`.

title: Pull updates from the remote
description: Pulling fetches changes from the remote and integrates them into your local branch. In a real team, others push commits while you work — you pull to stay in sync. Pull the latest changes into your local `main` branch.
hint: From inside the `practice` folder: `git pull origin main`. If you are already in sync, check with `git fetch origin && git log origin/main --oneline`.

title: Resolve a merge conflict
description: Conflicts happen when two branches change the same line of the same file differently — Git cannot decide which to keep, so it marks the file and asks you to resolve it manually. Create two branches that each edit the same line differently, merge one into the other, fix the conflict markers (`<<<<<<<`, `=======`, `>>>>>>>`), stage the resolved file, and complete the merge with a commit.
hint: Edit the same line in two branches. Merge one into the other. Open the conflicted file, remove the markers, keep what you want, then `git add` and `git commit`.
